design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA and SWiM; protocol registered on the Open Science Framework in May 2024, 10.17605/OSF.IO/K9NTY) of studies relating the alcohol hangover to negative affect (anxiety, low mood, stress, guilt, emotional dysregulation) in healthy adults, compared with a sober state or baseline. 22 studies (n = 6152): randomized and semi-naturalistic experiments, naturalistic within-person studies, cross-sectional surveys and three interview studies, synthesized narratively by theme. Risk of bias with RoB 2, ROBINS-I, the AXIS tool for cross-sectional studies and the CASP qualitative checklist.
can_establish: Which negative feelings people report the day after drinking compared with sober days or baseline, how consistently the direction of the difference appears across designs, which personal characteristics have been studied alongside it, and how people describe the experience in interviews.
cannot_establish: How large the change in mood is (no effect sizes are reported or pooled), whether the mood change is caused by the hangover itself or by sleep loss, events of the night, expectations or pre-existing mood (mostly naturalistic and cross-sectional designs), or whether any personal factor or coping strategy changes it (associations from single cross-sectional or small studies).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Included studies: mostly young adults recruited from the general population, with 10 of 22 specifically recruiting students; most from the United Kingdom (9) and the United States (5), published 1980 to 2024 (p. 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy adults aged 18 or over with experience of a hangover; a validated hangover measure or descriptive self-report of a hangover; a relationship between hangover and negative affect; a comparison with a sober state or baseline. Excluded: reviews, grey literature and conference papers, participants under 18, current alcohol dependence, hangovers combined with other substances, no hangover-specific measure (pp. 2-3).
sample.demographics: 57% women (3531 of 6152); ages 18 to 88; mean age 26.3 (SD 7.9) in the 16 studies that reported it; individual samples from 11 to 1837 (p. 3).
sample.selection_effects: Mostly students and young adults with mild-to-moderate hangovers; people with alcohol dependence excluded; English-language peer-reviewed studies only. The largest samples are retrospective surveys.

exposure.measurement: Hangover measured with a single-item severity rating (10 studies), the Alcohol Hangover Severity Scale (7) or other scales, or by asking about a recent hangover (p. 3).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: reported average consumption from 6 to 17 alcoholic units depending on the timeframe; mean units per drinking session in Table 4 from 10.6 to 19.7; estimated peak blood alcohol up to 0.22%; in the randomized trials hangover severity was weak (for example 1.4 on single-item or acute hangover scales) (p. 3; Table 4, pp. 11-12).
exposure.polysubstance: Studies combining alcohol with other substances (for example alcohol and cannabis) were excluded; other drug use in the remaining studies not summarized.

comparison.controls: A sober day or alcohol-free condition in the same people (experimental and naturalistic studies), baseline affect, or variation in hangover severity across respondents (cross-sectional surveys).
comparison.matching: Within-person comparisons in most experimental and naturalistic studies; none in the surveys.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The authors name tolerance, sleep and pre-existing psychological conditions as unmeasured differences (p. 15); one included study suggests baseline anxiety re-emerges during hangover (p. 14).

outcomes.instruments: State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (4 studies), visual analogue mood scales (8), Profile of Mood States, Beck Depression Inventory II, Depression Anxiety Stress Scales, Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (state and trait versions), Brief-COPE, Brief Resilience Scale, single-item ratings; semi-structured and unstructured interviews (Table 1, pp. 5-7).
outcomes.validity_norms: Mostly validated scales; several single-item ratings.
outcomes.operationalization: Negative affect as higher anxiety, depression, stress, guilt or irritability, or lower positive mood, during a hangover than when sober or at baseline.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; outcomes are self-reported, usually by participants who knew whether they were hungover.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The review reports direction and significance as stated in each study (Table 4, pp. 11-12) and themes from the qualitative studies (Table 5, p. 13); no standardized effect, interval or pooled estimate is given, because measures and analyses were too heterogeneous (p. 3).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Open Science Framework, registered prospectively in May 2024 (10.17605/OSF.IO/K9NTY); search on 20 January 2025 (p. 2); deviations not discussed.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not assessable; vote counting by significance as reported in each study.
analysis.power: Not applicable; included studies ranged from 11 to 1837 participants.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across most quantitative studies, people rated their mood as worse (more anxiety, low mood, stress, guilt, irritability and less alertness or contentment) during a hangover than when sober or at baseline; in the largest survey, anxiety and depression were the least reported and least severe hangover symptoms, two smaller studies found no difference in anxiety or tension, and the size of the change is never quantified. Associations with emotion regulation, repetitive negative thinking, baseline anxiety, coping style and resilience come from one or two studies each, mostly cross-sectional. In interviews, people linked their distress to what they had done while drunk, memory gaps and a wasted day, and said that sharing the hangover with friends eased it.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract (p. 1) says the 22 studies demonstrated a significant association, that maladaptive emotion regulation, avoidant coping, repetitive negative thinking and baseline anxiety exacerbated these experiences, and that social support and resilience were protective; the conclusion speaks of a strong link. Three of the 22 are interview studies, several found no difference for anxiety, no magnitude is reported, and the causal words (exacerbated, protective) rest on correlational single studies.

timeline.event: McKinney, narrative review of next-day effects of alcohol on subjective mood: overall decrease in mood with more anxiety and fatigue during hangover (cited as ref. 16; not in the library's references).
Gunn et al., systematic review of next-day effects of heavy drinking on cognition (a related outcome, cited as ref. 10)
This review: negative affect higher during hangover in most of 19 quantitative studies, with no pooled magnitude.

replication.where_it_stands: The direction (worse mood during a hangover) is consistent across many small studies and with the earlier review, but its size, and whether it is caused by the hangover itself rather than by sleep loss or regret about the night, are not established.

funding.funder: No specific funding for the work; the first author held an Australian Government Research Training Program scholarship (pp. 1, 16).
funding.declared_conflicts: A.C.H. was supported by a Rebecca L Cooper Al and Val Rosenstrauss Fellowship (GNT: F2021894); the other authors declare no conflicts (p. 16).
funding.affiliations_note: Centre for Human Psychopharmacology, Swinburne University of Technology; Institute for Breathing and Sleep, Austin Hospital, Melbourne.

what_would_settle_it: A within-person study with randomized alcohol and placebo-alcohol nights, repeated standardized mood measures the next day, sleep measured objectively, and analysis of how much mood change remains after accounting for sleep loss and events of the night; plus a trial of any proposed way to ease next-day anxiety.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two critical items are not met (4, the narrow single-person search with unjustified restrictions, and 7, no list of excluded studies), and one is met only in part (9), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2. The more important limitation for the site is that the review reports no magnitudes: it can support a claim about the direction of mood change during a hangover, with very low certainty, but not about how large the change is or what causes it. Its moderator findings rest on single cross-sectional studies and its qualitative findings are themes, not frequencies.

key_findings.finding: 22 studies with 6152 participants were included (individual samples 11 to 1837; 57% women; ages 18 to 88; mean age 26.3, SD 7.9, in the 16 studies reporting it); 10 recruited students; no meta-analysis was done because measures and analyses were heterogeneous.
key_findings.locator: 2.5 Data Extraction, last sentences; 3.1 Overview of Included Studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Across the quantitative studies, participants reported more negative affect during a hangover than when sober or at baseline: more anxiety, depression, stress, anger, agitation, irritability, regret, apathy, guilt and escapism, and less alertness, tranquillity and contentment.

In the largest survey (1837 students), anxiety and depression were the least reported and least severe hangover symptoms, while regret and apathy had moderate severity; one study found no significant effect on tension-anxiety, one found no change in anxiety or depression among people who rarely get hangovers, and one found no difference in anxiety between dark and clear spirits.
key_findings.locator: 3.3.1, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Table 4, rows Hogewoning 2016, Mackus 2023, van Schrojenstein Lantman 2017, Collins 1980

key_findings.finding: In the randomized trials, hangovers were weak (mean severity 1.4 on a single-item scale and 1.4 on the Acute Hangover Scale), and estimated or measured blood alcohol ranged up to 0.22% in the naturalistic studies.

Greater emotional dysregulation during hangover than when sober was found in three studies; in one study emotional dysregulation and repetitive negative thinking predicted depressive (not anxiety) symptoms during hangover and baseline anxiety correlated with hangover anxiety; in one cross-sectional survey depression, anxiety, stress and avoidant coping correlated positively, and resilience negatively, with hangover severity.

In three interview studies (66, 23 and 20 participants), people described sadness, anger, regret, guilt, shame, dread, embarrassment and worry during hangovers, mostly prompted by behaviour while drunk that clashed with their values, partial memory loss and a wasted day; they said that sharing the hangover with friends who had also been drinking eased their distress; in one study low mood lingered longer than the physical symptoms.
key_findings.locator: 3.3.2 Qualitative Findings; Table 5 (p. 13); Table 1 sample sizes (pp. 5-7)

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias: almost all non-randomized studies moderate, three serious; cross-sectional studies 76% preferred responses on the AXIS tool, none justifying sample size or addressing non-response; qualitative studies 87% yes on CASP; all three randomized trials rated low overall.
The authors note that people tend to adopt short-term strategies to lessen hangovers, such as drinking water or eating before drinking, rather than reducing how much they drink.

reporting_issues.issue: The design counts (5 experimental, 15 observational including 10 naturalistic and 5 cross-sectional, and 3 qualitative) add up to 23, not 22; Table 1 lists nine naturalistic studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: One naturalistic study is double-counted in the text (Table 1, pp. 5-7).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the mean age as 26.9 years, the Results as 26.3 (SD 7.9).
All three randomized trials are rated low risk overall although two were judged to have some concerns about selective reporting.
reporting_issues.consequence: Under RoB 2 the overall judgment cannot be milder than the worst domain; these two trials should be some concerns.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says all cross-sectional studies reported funding or conflicts, but Table 2 marks this item as unknown for Harburg et al. (1993).

In Table 4 the row for Gunn et al. (2021) cites references 40 and 42 (reference 40 is a 2019 study by Devenney et al.) and shows exactly the same drinking, blood alcohol and hangover values as Hudson and Gunn (2023), each with 45 participants.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two entries appear to describe the same sample, which would count its participants twice in the 6152 total.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 describes Terpstra et al. (2022) as a survey of 648 students with a mean age of 47.8 (SD 18.2) (checked on the rendered page).
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the population label or the age is wrong; the coping and resilience findings should not be described as coming from students.
